Executive Summary and Legislative Evolution (2024–2026)

Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program represents the foundational pillar of federal industrial and technological policy, delivering multi-billion-dollar annual support to enterprises conducting scientific research and experimental development within Canadian jurisdiction. Administered jointly through legislative policy established by the Department of Finance Canada and operational enforcement executed by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the program operates through a dual-mechanism statutory framework codified under the federal Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)). First, taxpayers are permitted to pool and immediately deduct eligible current expenditures and—effective December 16, 2024—eligible capital SR&ED expenditures against business income under Section 37. Second, taxpayers earn Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under Section 127 and refundable ITCs under Section 127.1, which either offset Part I federal income tax otherwise payable or provide direct cash refunds to qualifying corporations and unincorporated businesses.

Following the initial announcement of a comprehensive statutory review in Budget 2022 and subsequent consultations in Budget 2024, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most profound structural transformation in over a decade between December 2024 and mid-2026. Initiated by policy measures unveiled in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement, refined through draft legislative proposals and explanatory notes released by the Department of Finance on August 15, 2025, expanded further in Budget 2025, and enacted into force via Bill C-15 (Statutes of Canada 2026, Chapter 3), the federal government fundamentally recalibrated the SR&ED regime. These legislative amendments directly addressed long-standing structural deficiencies regarding the premature phase-out of scaling domestic technology firms, the exclusion of public growth corporations from refundable incentives, and the post-2013 prohibition on capital equipment claims.

Concurrently, provincial jurisdictions have enacted major structural reforms to their complementary R&D tax regimes, creating a highly dynamic multi-jurisdictional incentive environment. Most notably, for taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec abolished six legacy R&D and design tax credits—including its flagship Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D)—and consolidated them into the new Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC), which introduces a universal 30% and 20% two-tier refundable rate structure and extends coverage to capital assets and pre-commercialization activities. Combined with Ontario's tri-pillar credit architecture—comprising the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), and the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC)—alongside Alberta's incremental Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) and Manitoba's partially refundable credit regime, Canadian corporate taxpayers must navigate an interdependent matrix of federal and provincial statutes.

body.text: Statutory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
Subsection 248(1): Statutory Definition, Eligible Support Work, and Explicit Exclusions

The legal gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". The statutory provision bifurcates qualifying core activities into three primary pillars, which are supplemented by a strictly circumscribed fourth category of eligible support work. Under Paragraph (a), basic research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Under Paragraph (b), applied research encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Under Paragraph (c), experimental development encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Because experimental development shares an application-oriented focus with applied research while targeting technological advancements in commercial industries, the overwhelming majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada are filed under Paragraph (c).

Once a taxpayer establishes that core basic research, applied research, or experimental development is being undertaken in Canada under Paragraphs (a), (b), or (c), Paragraph (d) of subsection 248(1) extends SR&ED eligibility to support work with respect to eight exhaustive functional categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research. Support work is never eligible as SR&ED on a standalone basis; rather, Paragraph (d) mandates that such activities qualify only where the work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core basic research, applied research, or experimental development work undertaken in Canada.

A critical legal nuance in audit defence lies in the statutory boundary between Paragraph (d) eligible support work and the explicit statutory exclusions enumerated in Paragraphs (e) through (k) of the subsection 248(1) definition. Specifically, the Income Tax Act mandates that SR&ED does not include work with respect to market research or sales promotion under Paragraph (e); quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes under Paragraph (f); research in the social sciences or the humanities under Paragraph (g); prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas under Paragraph (h); the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process under Paragraph (i); style changes under Paragraph (j); or routine data collection under Paragraph (k).

As the CRA's administrative guidelines emphasize, distinguishing between eligible Paragraph (d) support work—such as testing or data collection—and excluded Paragraphs (f) and (k) work—such as routine testing or routine data collection—depends entirely on the underlying purpose for which the activity was performed. When data collection or testing is carried out for commercial quality assurance, regulatory sign-off, or standard operational monitoring, it falls within the statutory exclusions and cannot be claimed. Conversely, when data collection, computer programming, or engineering testing is executed specifically for the purpose of testing a scientific or technological hypothesis and is commensurate with the needs of resolving a technological uncertainty in Canada, it qualifies in full as eligible support work under Paragraph (d). Similarly, if a mining or energy enterprise conducts eligible experimental development while simultaneously prospecting for minerals, the taxpayer may file an SR&ED claim for the experimental development work, but must strictly segregate and exclude all mineral prospecting activities pursuant to Paragraph (h).

body.text: Section 37: The Deductible SR&ED Expenditure Pool and International Wage Limits

Once technical activities satisfy the subsection 248(1) threshold, Section 37 of the Income Tax Act governs the deductibility of the associated expenditures in computing income from a business carried on by the taxpayer. Rather than requiring taxpayers to amortize R&D outlays over multiple fiscal periods or capitalize them to specific intangible assets, subsection 37(1) establishes an evergreen pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Taxpayers may elect to deduct any portion of the positive balance of this pool against business income in the current taxation year or carry the unclaimed pool balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years, with continuity rules under paragraph 87(2)(j.6) preserving pool balances across qualifying corporate amalgamations and wind-ups.

The composition of the Section 37(1) pool is governed by a precise hierarchy of statutory paragraphs and subsections. Paragraph 37(1)(a) captures expenditures of a current nature made by the taxpayer on SR&ED carried on in Canada, encompassing work directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), payments to arm's-length subcontractors under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), and third-party payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or non-profit R&D corporations related to the taxpayer's class of business under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) to (iii). Enacted via Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), Paragraph 37(1)(b) restores the immediate deductibility of eligible capital expenditures—specifically the acquisition of depreciable property other than buildings or leasehold interests in buildings—acquired on or after December 16, 2024, for use in SR&ED carried on in Canada.

To prevent double-dipping on subsidized expenditures, Paragraphs 37(1)(d) and (e) mandate that the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures be reduced by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED. Furthermore, any federal SR&ED ITC claimed against tax payable or refunded in cash in a preceding taxation year reduces the Section 37(1) pool in the subsequent taxation year, and if the reduction exceeds the available pool balance, the negative balance is included in business income under paragraph 12(1)(t) or 12(1)(v).

While SR&ED expenditures incurred outside Canada are generally governed by subsection 37(2)—which permits a current-year deduction against income but excludes those outlays from the Section 37(1) pool and denies any Section 127 ITC—subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) establish a vital statutory exception for permissible foreign salaries and wages. Under subsection 37(1.4), where a Canadian-resident employee performs SR&ED work outside Canada that is solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada, those salaries and wages may be included in the Section 37(1) pool and qualify for Section 127 ITCs, subject to a strict ceiling under subsection 37(1.5) equal to 10% of the total salaries and wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada during the taxation year. Finally, subsection 37(8) provides the overarching interpretive rules determining which expenditures are incurred in respect of SR&ED under the traditional overhead method versus the proxy method, including subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(II)—which was amended to apply to capital property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, and lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024—and subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V), which governs materials transformed under the proxy method.
Sections 127 and 127.1: Investment Tax Credits, Qualified Expenditures, and Refundability

Whereas Section 37 governs income deductibility, Section 127 and Section 127.1 govern the calculation, application, carryforward, recapture, and refundability of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits. Under subsection 127(5), a taxpayer may deduct their available ITC pool against Part I federal income tax otherwise payable. Any unused non-refundable ITCs earned in a taxation year may be carried back 3 taxation years to recover prior Part I taxes paid, or carried forward up to 20 taxation years (increased from 10 years pursuant to the May 2, 2006 federal budget for taxation years ending after 2005).

The statutory base upon which SR&ED ITCs are computed is the taxpayer's "qualified expenditure" pool for the taxation year, as defined in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act. Practitioners must account for three structural divergences between the Section 37(1) deductible expenditure pool and the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool. First, where a taxpayer elects to use the proxy method for overhead under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B), the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount—calculated at 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations—is added to qualified expenditures for Section 127 ITC purposes, even though it is never added to the Section 37(1) deductible expenditure pool. Second, under paragraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), expenditures for SR&ED performed on behalf of the taxpayer by arm's-length subcontractors or paid as third-party payments (described in subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) to (iii)) are restricted to 80% of the actual expenditure amount when computing the ITC base. Third, payments to non-arm's-length subcontractors are excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures (subject to special qualified expenditure transfer agreements under subsections 127(13) to (20)), and any salary or wages unpaid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year are barred under subsection 78(4) until the taxation year in which they are actually paid.

Under subsections 127(9) and 127(10.1), operating in tandem with the refundability rules of Section 127.1, federal SR&ED ITCs function as a two-tier incentive structure. At the basic tier, all corporations, unincorporated individuals, and trusts earn a base 15% ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures. For corporations that are neither Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) nor Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—such as foreign-controlled Canadian subsidiaries or large public corporations exceeding the revenue phase-out—this 15% basic ITC is strictly non-refundable. For unincorporated individuals, certain trusts, and qualifying CCPCs or ECPCs incurring expenditures above their annual expenditure limit, the 15% basic ITC is 40% refundable under Section 127.1, yielding an effective cash refund of 6% of excess qualified expenditures. At the enhanced tier, subsection 127(10.1) provides an additional 20% ITC on top of the 15% basic rate for qualifying CCPCs and—for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024—qualifying ECPCs, resulting in a total enhanced ITC of 35% on qualified expenditures up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit. Under Section 127.1 and subsection 127.1(2.01), this 35% enhanced ITC earned within the annual expenditure limit is 100% refundable in respect of current expenditures and 40% refundable in respect of restored capital expenditures.
The 2024–2026 Federal SR&ED Reforms: Rates, Thresholds, and Capital Restoration
Expansion of the Enhanced 35% Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Mechanics

The cornerstone of the 2024–2026 legislative reforms enacted in Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3) is the doubling of the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC alongside a substantial expansion of the phase-out corridors. Although the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement and the August 15, 2025 draft legislative proposals initially contemplated raising the annual expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million, Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 increased the statutory limit to $6 million, effective retroactively for all taxation years that begin on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024). As a direct result, a qualifying CCPC or ECPC incurring $6 million in eligible current SR&ED expenditures can now secure up to $2.1 million in 100% refundable federal cash credits annually, doubling the historical $1.05 million ceiling.

Simultaneously, Parliament overhauled the phase-out formula in subsection 127(10.2) for CCPCs utilizing the taxable capital method. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, a CCPC's $3 million expenditure limit began decreasing once its taxable capital employed in Canada for the preceding taxation year—aggregated across all associated CCPCs under subsection 127(10.21)—reached $10 million, and was completely eliminated at $50 million, representing a $40 million phase-out range that is preserved on Part 10A of the 2026 Form T661. For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, the taxable capital phase-out floor has been raised from $10 million to $15 million and the upper elimination threshold has been increased from $50 million to $75 million, establishing a $60 million phase-out corridor. Under amended subsection 127(10.2), the annual expenditure limit for a stand-alone CCPC (or an associated group of CCPCs under subsection 127(10.21)) that does not make the gross revenue election is determined by the following statutory formula:

Expenditure limit = $6 million × [($60 million − A) ÷ $60 million], where A is nil if the corporation's taxable capital employed in Canada for the preceding taxation year (aggregated across associated corporations) is $15 million or less, and otherwise the lesser of $60 million and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15 million.

Under this statutory formula, every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada in excess of $15 million reduces the $6 million expenditure limit by $1, until the expenditure limit reaches nil at $75 million of taxable capital. Where a CCPC has a short taxation year or is associated with other CCPCs having multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year, specific proration and anti-avoidance determination rules apply under subsection 127(10.64) and renumbered subsection 127(10.5).
Extension to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the Gross Revenue Election

Historically, the moment a Canadian private technology, biotechnology, or clean-energy enterprise executed an Initial Public Offering (IPO) or reverse takeover on a public stock exchange, it ceased to be a CCPC—triggering a deemed taxation year-end, slashing its federal SR&ED ITC rate from 35% to 15%, and eliminating 100% cash refundability. To remove this structural penalty against domestic public market capitalization, amended subsection 127(10.1) and newly enacted subsections 127(10.6) through 127(10.64) extend the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024.

To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year, a corporation must satisfy three cumulative statutory requirements. First, the corporation must be resident in Canada throughout the year. Second, the corporation must have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange, or have validly elected or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue to be a public corporation. Third, the corporation must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons.

Because public corporations routinely raise substantial equity capital on public markets that would prematurely disqualify them under a balance-sheet taxable capital metric, subsection 127(10.6) determines an ECPC's $6 million expenditure limit using a phase-out formula based exclusively on average annual gross revenue over the preceding three fiscal years. Where an ECPC is a member of a consolidated corporate group that prepares consolidated financial statements—defined in subsection 127(9) as financial statements in which the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the group members are presented as those of a single economic entity—subsections 127(10.61) to 127(10.63) mandate that the $6 million expenditure limit be shared among the consolidated ECPC group members using the consolidated group's annual revenue, paralleling the allocation and failure-to-file mechanisms for associated CCPCs under subsections 127(10.21), 127(10.3), and 127(10.4).

Crucially, under new subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), a stand-alone CCPC or a group of associated CCPCs is now permitted to file an election with the Minister of National Revenue—executed in Part 9 of the 2026 Form T661—to opt out of the taxable capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) and instead compute its expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average gross revenue structure. If an associated CCPC group elects this method, the calculation uses the total average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of each corporation that is a member of the associated group for the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether those corporations were associated throughout that entire three-year period. For venture-backed Canadian private corporations in capital-intensive industries—such as life sciences, clean technology, robotics, and semiconductor development—that accumulate over $15 million or even over $75 million in paid-up capital and debt long before generating commercial revenue, electing the gross revenue method under subsection 127(10.31) or 127(10.32) preserves 100% of their $6 million enhanced refundable expenditure limit.
Reinstatement of Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Between January 1, 2014, and December 15, 2024, capital expenditures and capital lease outlays were completely excluded from the SR&ED program pursuant to legislative repeals enacted in the Jobs and Growth Act, 2012 (S.C. 2012, c. 31, s. 27). Effective in respect of depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 (after December 15, 2024) and, in the case of lease costs, in respect of amounts that first become payable on or after December 16, 2024, Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3) restores the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures for both immediate income deduction under paragraph 37(1)(b) and ITC generation under Section 127. Simultaneously, paragraph 127(11.1)(c.1) was repealed as obsolete for property acquired on or after December 16, 2024.

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy and the amended provisions of the Income Tax Act, claimants must satisfy rigorous ownership, intent, timing, and utilization criteria. Eligible SR&ED capital expenditures are strictly limited to the acquisition of depreciable property—defined as property for which Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) could otherwise be claimed under paragraph 20(1)(a)—in which the claimant acquires freehold ownership or a valid leasehold interest. Buildings and leasehold interests in buildings remain statutorily excluded from SR&ED capital treatment. Moreover, if a claimant incurs costs to construct a structure on land owned by another party without acquiring ownership or a leasehold interest in the asset, or holds property merely as an agent or nominee for another party, CCA cannot be claimed and the outlay is barred as an SR&ED capital expenditure. In the case of partnerships, subsection 96(1) of the Income Tax Act and subsection 1102(1a) of the Income Tax Regulations require that partnership SR&ED property be accounted for at the partnership level.

To qualify for full immediate deduction under paragraph 37(1)(b) and full ITC inclusion under subsection 127(9), the newly acquired depreciable property must satisfy the "all or substantially all" test: it must be intended either to be used all or substantially all (defined administratively by the CRA as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in the performance of SR&ED in Canada, covering R&D laboratory and testing equipment, prototyping machinery, specialized tools, and development infrastructure. Where depreciable machinery and equipment is used primarily—meaning between 50% and 90% of its operating time—for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, it qualifies under the restored shared-use equipment rules, which permit partial ITC claims over the asset's initial operating terms without granting a 100% upfront deduction against income under paragraph 37(1)(b).

Furthermore, claimants must navigate two vital operational rules governing timing and cash refundability. First, under amended subsection 127(11.2), capital property is deemed not to have been acquired for ITC purposes until it is considered available for use by the taxpayer in the performance of SR&ED, creating a critical distinction between the date an expenditure is incurred for paragraph 37(1)(b) deductibility and the date the property becomes available for use under subsection 127(11.2). Second, under amended Section 127.1 and subsection 127.1(2.01), while a qualifying CCPC or ECPC receives a 100% cash refund on the 35% enhanced ITC earned on current expenditures, the statutory rate of refundability on the 35% enhanced ITC (as well as on the 15% basic ITC) earned on SR&ED expenditures of a capital nature is fixed at 40%. If a taxpayer subsequently sells the SR&ED capital property or converts its use to commercial production, the ITC recapture rules under subsections 127(27) to (35) and CCA recapture rules apply to recover the previously claimed tax incentives.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Calculation Methods, and Specified Employees
Direct Salaries, Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Materials

The accurate identification and computation of Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) requires strict adherence to the CRA's expenditure policies and the statutory distinctions between direct labour, materials, and external contractors under Sections 37, 78, 127, and 248 of the Income Tax Act. Eligible salaries or wages encompass employment income as defined in subsection 248(1) and computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act, paid to employees for the proportion of their time directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, plus permissible foreign support wages up to the 10% ceiling under subsection 37(1.5). In computing eligible SR&ED salaries and wages, claimants must exclude the value of non-cash taxable benefits, employee stock option benefits, and any Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST) input tax credits or Provincial Sales Tax (PST) rebates claimed by the employer on employee taxable benefits, as subsection 248(16) deems such input tax credits and rebates to be government assistance. Furthermore, under subsection 78(4), any accrued salary, wage, or bonus that remains unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year; rather, it is deemed to be incurred—and may be reported on Line 310 of Form T661—only in the subsequent taxation year in which it is actually paid.

With respect to physical inputs, claimants may deduct and claim ITCs at 100% on the cost of materials that are either consumed—meaning rendered virtually valueless or destroyed during experimentation—or transformed, meaning incorporated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or product during the prosecution of SR&ED (eligible under both the traditional and proxy methods since February 23, 1998, pursuant to subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V)). However, if materials transformed into an experimental prototype or pilot asset are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, ITC recapture rules apply to claw back the tax credit attributable to the lesser of the proceeds of disposition (or fair market value upon conversion) and the original cost of the transformed materials claimed.

Where a claimant contracts out eligible SR&ED work to an arm's-length Canadian subcontractor under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), or makes third-party payments to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or research consortia for SR&ED related to the taxpayer's class of business under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) to (iii), 100% of the expenditure is deductible in the Section 37(1) pool, but paragraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) restricts the ITC base to 80% of the contract or third-party expenditure. Simultaneously, the Canadian contractor performing the SR&ED on behalf of the payer must reduce its own SR&ED expenditure pool by the contract amount received or receivable under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(9) to prevent duplicate claims on the same underlying R&D activity.
Overhead Methodologies: Traditional Method vs. Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)

To account for overhead and indirect support expenditures associated with R&D operations, a taxpayer must make an annual, irrevocable election on Form T661—applicable across all SR&ED projects claimed in that taxation year—between the Traditional Method under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and the Proxy Method under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B).

body.text: Under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) has been set at 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base since the 2014 taxation year, following the historical step-down from 65% in 2012 and prior years and 60% in 2013. The actual overhead expenses represented by the PPA—including office supplies, general-purpose office equipment, heat, water, electricity, telephones, salaries or wages for administrative and clerical support staff, travel, training, property taxes, and routine maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment—remain deductible as ordinary business expenses, but are not added to the Section 37(1) pool. Instead, the notional 55% PPA calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 is transferred directly to Line 820 in Part 8 of Form T661 to expand the qualified expenditure pool for Section 127 ITC purposes. Because the Traditional Method requires granular, invoice-by-invoice accounting proof that every claimed overhead dollar on Line 360 was both directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED—meaning the expense would not have been incurred had the SR&ED not been carried out—most Canadian technology, software, and engineering enterprises elect the Proxy Method.
Restrictions and Salary Base Caps for Specified Employees

To prevent closely held corporations from inflating their SR&ED claims and the 55% PPA through owner-manager remuneration, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose strict statutory limitations on "specified employees"—defined in subsection 248(1) as employees who are specified shareholders (owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation) or who do not deal at arm's length with the employer. First, for all employees regardless of shareholding status, subsection 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations excludes four specific items from the PPA salary base on Line 502 of Form T661: taxable benefits, prior-year unpaid salaries or wages paid in the current taxation year (Line 310), bonuses, and remuneration based on profits.

Second, for each specified employee, subsection 2900(7) of the Income Tax Regulations restricts the maximum amount that a claimant can include in the PPA salary base to the lesser of two statutory ceilings. The first ceiling is 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages from the claimant for the year—encompassing both SR&ED and non-SR&ED duties, but excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid amounts paid in the year. The second ceiling is determined by the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) formula set out in subsection 2900(7):

In this statutory formula, A represents the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) as determined for Canada Pension Plan (CPP) purposes for the calendar year in which the claimant's taxation year ends, and B represents the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual, with no proration for any portion of the year during which the employee was not yet a specified employee. Where a specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations during the year, additional allocation rules apply across the associated group, requiring the corporations to allocate the salary limit using Form T1174, Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED).
Program Administration, Filing Procedures, and Compliance Governance
Governing Authorities, Form T661 Structure, and Schedule T2SCH31

While the Department of Finance Canada holds exclusive authority over statutory drafting and tax policy under the Income Tax Act, the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) administers the federal SR&ED program as well as the harmonized provincial and territorial R&D tax credits for Ontario, British Columbia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, and Yukon. To claim federal SR&ED tax incentives, a corporate taxpayer must file Form T661, Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, alongside Schedule T2SCH31, Investment Tax Credit – Corporations (while unincorporated individuals file Form T661 alongside Form T2038(IND), Investment Tax Credit (Individuals), and partnerships file Form T661 with their T5013 partnership information return). Following the enactment of Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), the CRA released the updated 2026 version of Form T661 on May 15, 2026, and the updated Schedule T2SCH31 on May 22, 2026, incorporating the reporting of depreciable capital property acquired after December 15, 2024, the CCPC gross revenue election, and the $6 million expenditure limit.

body.text: Statutory Filing Deadlines, Pre-Claim Approval, and Preparer Penalties

Compliance with the statutory SR&ED filing deadline is an absolute condition precedent to entitlement under the Income Tax Act. Under paragraph 150(1)(a), a Canadian corporation's T2 income tax return filing due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year. Pursuant to subsections 37(11) and 127(9), a corporation is granted an additional 12 months beyond its T2 filing due date—resulting in a strict statutory deadline of 18 months from the end of the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred—to file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 containing all prescribed information. Unincorporated individuals have 17.5 months from the end of the taxation year to report their SR&ED expenditures on Form T661 and Form T2038(IND). If a claimant takes more than the additional 12 months allowed after the return filing due date to submit the prescribed forms, the taxpayer is statutorily barred from deducting the SR&ED expenditures under Section 37 and is ineligible to earn any ITCs under Section 127 for those outlays.

To ensure transparency and deter abusive contingency-fee arrangements, Part 9 of Form T661 requires complete disclosure of the name, Business Number, billing arrangement, and fee of any person or firm that accepts consideration to prepare or assist in preparing the SR&ED claim. Under subsection 162(5.1) of the Income Tax Act, if required claim preparer information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or false, a $1,000 penalty is assessed per SR&ED claim, for which the claimant corporation and the claim preparer are jointly and severally liable.

Beginning in 2025 and expanding across 2026, the CRA also implemented a comprehensive administrative modernization program to make SR&ED compliance more predictable and less burdensome. Key operational reforms include the launch of a voluntary pre-claim approval program—which provides eligible businesses whose gross business income is below $25 million with binding upfront certainty on project eligibility prior to filing their tax return—alongside AI-supported claim screening to fast-track low-risk claims without unnecessary audit delays, a streamlined review process with reduced documentation burdens, and updated CRA policy publications on salary and wages, filing requirements, and penalties.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Incentive Regimes
Government Assistance Interaction and Federal Pool Reduction Mechanics

Every Canadian province (with the exception of Prince Edward Island) and the Yukon territory provides a provincial or territorial R&D tax credit or tax-delivered grant program that stacks atop the federal SR&ED regime. Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) of the federal Income Tax Act, all provincial R&D tax credits and grants are legally classified as "government assistance". Consequently, any provincial R&D incentive that a taxpayer receives, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive reduces both the federal Section 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and the federal subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool for the taxation year.

Because the federal 35% or 15% ITC is calculated on qualified expenditures net of provincial government assistance—while the 55% federal Prescribed Proxy Amount is unaffected by the provincial credit reduction—the combined federal-provincial effective rate on direct expenditure dollars follows an interdependent multiplicative interaction:
Combined effective rate = P + [F × (1 − P)], where P is the provincial credit rate and F is the federal ITC rate (35% or 15%)

Where a taxpayer claims the 55% PPA on direct SR&ED labour, the federal ITC is further augmented by up to 19.25% (35% × 55%) on the eligible salary base, resulting in combined federal-provincial cash recovery rates that frequently exceed 50% of gross R&D payroll in jurisdictions such as Québec and Ontario.

body.text: Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Ontario operates a comprehensive three-credit R&D incentive architecture under the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), administered on behalf of the Ontario Ministry of Finance by the CRA through the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. The first pillar is the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC), claimed on Schedule 566, which provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit (for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016; previously 10% before June 1, 2016) on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario up to an annual expenditure limit of $3 million, yielding a maximum annual refund of $240,000. Unlike the federal SR&ED regime, Ontario has retained a dual phase-out mechanism for the $3 million OITC expenditure limit: the limit phases out when the corporation's prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000, or when its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25 million and $50 million.

The second pillar is the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), claimed on Schedule 508, which provides a 3.5% non-refundable corporate income tax credit on eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario to reduce Ontario corporate income tax payable. Because both the OITC and the ORDTC constitute government assistance that reduces the federal Section 37 deductible pool and the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool—whereas Ontario credits do not reduce each other unless specified by the provincial calculation order—an unprofitable CCPC that cannot immediately utilize the non-refundable 3.5% ORDTC would otherwise suffer a reduction in its 35% federal cash refund. To remedy this friction, Ontario law permits a corporation to waive the tax credit, or a portion of the tax credit, by delivering a written waiver with its T2 return on or before six months after its taxation year-end, or on an amended return for that year.

The third pillar is the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC), governed by section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) and claimed on Schedule 568 alongside a separate Schedule 569 (Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit Contract Information) for each eligible contract, with the total claimed credit entered on Line 470 of Schedule 5 (Tax Calculation Supplementary – Corporations). The OBRITC provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified current SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract entered into after May 6, 1997, with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI)—including Ontario universities, Ontario colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes at large teaching hospitals, Ontario Centres of Excellence, Networks of Centres of Excellence operating in Ontario, and designated non-profit research organizations. To qualify, the corporation must carry on business through a permanent establishment in Ontario, must not be exempt from tax under Part III of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), must make the expenditure as a payment of money rather than a payment-in-kind, must be entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED in its business, and must not be connected to the ERI (meaning the ERI cannot own shares carrying more than 10% of voting rights or 10% of the fair market value of issued shares, cannot be a partner or non-arm's-length party, and cannot hold shares through a partnership). Qualified expenditures for the OBRITC are subject to an annual cap of $20 million—which must be allocated among associated corporations in Part 3 of Schedule 568 pursuant to subsection 38(4) of Ontario Regulation 37/09—yielding a maximum annual refundable tax credit of $4 million ($20 million × 20%). Notably, small businesses may claim both the 20% OBRITC and the 8% OITC (as well as the federal SR&ED ITC) on the same qualified research contract expenditures.
Québec: The 2025 CRIC Consolidation vs. Legacy R&D Tax Credits

Like Alberta, Québec administers its corporate income tax and R&D tax incentives autonomously, through its provincial revenue agency, Revenu Québec. For taxation years and partnership fiscal periods beginning on or before March 25, 2025, Québec operated a fragmented suite of refundable R&D tax credits, requiring claimants to file Form RD-222-V (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures) alongside specific credit schedules including Form RD-1029.7-V (Tax Credit for Salaries and Wages (R&D)), Form RD-1029.8.6-V (Tax Credit for University Research or Research Carried Out by a Public Research Centre or a Research Consortium), and Form RD-1029.8.16.1-V (Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research).

For taxation years of corporations or fiscal periods of partnerships beginning after March 25, 2025, the Québec government enacted a historic consolidation by eliminating seven existing tax measures: the tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers (R&D); the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium; the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium; the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research; the tax credit for technological adaptation services; the industrial design component of the design tax credits; and the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts. In their place, effective for taxation years and fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, Québec introduced the unified Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (CRIC).

The CRIC regime introduces four major structural enhancements that make Québec one of the most lucrative R&D jurisdictions in North America. First, CRIC replaces the legacy asset-based rate phase-out with a universal two-tier refundable rate structure available to all qualified corporations regardless of size: a 30% refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures above the exclusion threshold, and a 20% refundable tax credit on all excess eligible expenditures above $1,000,000. Second, in addition to salaries and wages, subcontractor consideration, and payments to research organizations for R&D, CRIC expands eligibility to include pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec—bridging the gap between experimental development and commercial market entry. Third, harmonizing with the federal post-December 15, 2024 capital restoration, CRIC makes capital expenditures for the acquisition of depreciable property used in Québec R&D and pre-commercialization activities—such as laboratory equipment, software development infrastructure, prototyping manufacturing machinery, and testing equipment—eligible for the 30% and 20% refundable credit. Fourth, CRIC introduces a modified exclusion threshold designed to focus tax assistance on higher-value-added jobs: for a taxation year or fiscal period, the exclusion threshold equals the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the R&D employees threshold and the pre-commercialization employees threshold, which is computed using the Québec basic personal amount per employee prorated by the employee's time devoted to eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities (for example, 10 full-time R&D employees in 2025 at a basic personal amount of $18,571 results in an exclusion threshold of $185,710, above which all qualifying outlays earn the 30% and 20% refundable credit). When stacked with the 35% federal SR&ED ITC, a Québec corporation incurring $2 million in eligible R&D expenditures can secure $700,000 in federal SR&ED credits alongside up to $500,000 in provincial CRIC credits (prior to exclusion threshold and government assistance adjustments), exceeding $1.2 million in combined non-dilutive support.
Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) and Incremental Base Calculation

Administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance (Tax and Revenue Administration) under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and detailed in Information Circular IEG-1R5 and the Guide to Claiming the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) provides a refundable corporate tax benefit of up to 20% on qualifying R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020, that match those eligible for the federal SR&ED program. Claimants file AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970 (List of Innovation Employment Grant Projects Carried Out in Alberta) with their Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1) within a statutory filing deadline of 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing due date.

The IEG operates through an incremental two-tier rate mechanism capped at $4,000,000 in annual eligible Alberta R&D expenditures. A qualified corporation earns an 8% base payment on eligible R&D spending carried out in Alberta up to the corporation's base level of spending, and an enhanced 20% payment (consisting of the 8% base rate plus an additional 12% incremental credit) on eligible R&D spending that exceeds the corporation's base level of spending, up to the $4 million annual expenditure cap. A corporation's base level of spending is determined by calculating the corporation's average qualifying R&D spending in Alberta over the immediately preceding two taxation years. To target support to small and medium-sized enterprises, the grant phases out incrementally for corporations whose taxable capital employed in Canada falls between $10 million and $50 million (with recent Alberta Small Business Deduction capital phase-out alignments noted between $13.93 million and $69.67 million), and any recapture of IEG creates or increases Alberta corporate tax otherwise payable.
Manitoba and Other Provincial Jurisdictions

In Manitoba, corporations carrying on business through a permanent establishment in the province can claim the Manitoba Research and Development Tax Credit, which is equal to 15% of eligible SR&ED expenditures incurred in Manitoba after April 11, 2017 (reduced from the prior 20% rate). For in-house R&D expenditures, one-half of the Manitoba credit (7.5%) is refundable, while the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable; for R&D conducted under contract with an eligible educational institution, the entire 15% credit is refundable. The statutory filing deadline for claiming the Manitoba credit is 1 year after the corporation's T2 filing due date, and claimants may also claim repayments of government assistance that previously reduced the allowable SR&ED expenditure pool. Additional provincial and territorial R&D tax credits administered by the CRA include the Saskatchewan R&D Tax Credit and the Yukon R&D Tax Credit (Form 5011-TC / YT479), each of which reduces the federal SR&ED expenditure pool as government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d).
Judicial Precedents, CRA Policy Guidelines, and Audit Defence
The Five Questions Jurisprudence vs. the CRA "Why and How" Framework

In Canadian tax jurisprudence, the authoritative legal standard for determining whether a project satisfies the definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act is the Five Questions framework established by the Tax Court of Canada. To discharge its evidentiary burden of proof on a balance of probabilities, a taxpayer must affirmatively establish: first, that there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedure; second, that the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty; third, that the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses; fourth, that the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, that a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed.

On August 13, 2021, the CRA replaced its 2015 eligibility policy documents with the consolidated Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. In the 2021 Guidelines, the CRA restructured the eligibility analysis into two overarching requirements: the "Why" requirement and the "How" requirement. Under the "Why" requirement, the work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement—meaning the work must attempt to resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved using current knowledge, standard practice, or routine engineering. The CRA Guidelines explicitly stipulate that acquiring available knowledge or know-how through training, on-the-job learning, hiring expert employees or consultants, or purchasing proprietary knowledge does not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve a technological advancement. Under the "How" requirement, the work must be conducted by means of a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology through experiment or analysis, which requires generating an idea or hypothesis consistent with known facts as a starting point, testing that hypothesis by experiment or analysis (allowing the hypothesis to evolve as testing progresses), developing logical conclusions based on the experimental results, and keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.
Landmark Tax Court of Canada Rulings on Software, Engineering, and Documentation

Decisions of the Tax Court of Canada demonstrate how the judiciary resolves disputes between taxpayers and CRA Research and Technology Advisors across software architecture, custom mechanical engineering, and food or chemical formulation. In Hypercube Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 65), the Tax Court addressed the eligibility of software development activities and the threshold required to prove technological uncertainty and systematic investigation in computer programming projects. Similarly, in Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6), the Tax Court examined custom mechanical engineering claims and reinforced the strict judicial boundary between routine engineering or trial-and-error problem solving on the one hand, and a systematic scientific investigation grounded in measurable hypothesis formulation and testing on the other. As the Tax Court has emphasized, an identifiable hypothesis—even if implicit—combined with scientific thoroughness such as a rigorous process of measuring and analyzing test results is essential to distinguish eligible SR&ED from ineligible trial-and-error engineering.

In Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King (2024 TCC 159), an appeal decided under the informal procedure, Justice Bodie of the Tax Court of Canada provided favourable clarification for SR&ED claimants on three recurring audit battlegrounds. In Manning Canning, the appellant conducted experimentation to control microbial growth and create a vinegar-based beverage that was shelf-stable at room temperature without compromising flavour, testing potassium sorbate, sodium benzoate, and ultimately a natural preservative called Chiber. The Minister of National Revenue denied the SR&ED claim, arguing that the preservatives were already known to competent professionals in food science, that the appellant had not conducted a systematic investigation, and that contemporaneous records were inadequate. Justice Bodie allowed the appeal and held that the project qualified in full as SR&ED, articulating three principles; because the appeal was heard under the informal procedure, section 18.28 of the Tax Court of Canada Act provides that the judgment shall not be treated as a precedent for any other case:

cells: Scientific or technological uncertainty can be established even where a publicly available solution or ingredient exists, provided it has never been used or proven in the specific technical context of the claimant's project.
Rebuts CRA RTA denials asserting that because individual components, APIs, or chemical agents are publicly known, their integration under novel constraints is "routine engineering".

Contemporaneous records are meant to track the hypotheses generated, experiments undertaken, and results obtained for the claimant's own team; they do not need to be written so that an outside stranger unfamiliar with the field could replicate the results.
Validates natural engineering records—such as electronic project boards, source code design logs, test protocols, and internal formulation notes—without requiring academic-style peer-review papers.
Enduring Primacy of the Five Questions

Notwithstanding the CRA's administrative adoption of the "Why and How" approach in its 2021 Guidelines, the Five Questions jurisprudence remains a valid, authoritative legal methodology in the Tax Court of Canada.
Claimants should structure Form T661 Part 2 narratives (Lines 242, 244, and 246) to simultaneously satisfy the CRA's "Why and How" framework and the Tax Court's Five Questions.

body.text: Strategic Conclusions and Tax Planning Implications

The convergence of the federal 2024–2026 SR&ED legislative reforms enacted under Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3) and Québec's 2025 CRIC consolidation has fundamentally altered the capital allocation, corporate structuring, and compliance calculus for innovative businesses operating across Canada. First, with respect to corporate structuring and expenditure limit optimization, the expansion of the federal enhanced 35% ITC expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million—combined with the widened $15 million to $75 million taxable capital phase-out corridor and the new subsection 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) elections for CCPCs to use the three-year average gross revenue method—eliminates the historical penalty against venture-backed, capital-intensive private corporations. Tax directors of CCPCs whose prior-year associated taxable capital exceeds $15 million must model both the taxable capital formula under subsection 127(10.2) and the gross revenue election under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32) in Part 9 and Part 10 of the 2026 Form T661 to preserve up to $2.1 million in annual refundable federal credits.

Second, Canadian public companies listed on the TSX, TSX Venture Exchange, or foreign designated exchanges should conduct an immediate legal review of their share registers and governance structures to confirm that they are resident in Canada and not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by non-residents, thereby qualifying as Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) under subsection 127(10.6) for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Qualifying ECPCs can now access the 35% enhanced refundable ITC on up to $6 million of annual SR&ED expenditures, transforming post-IPO R&D cash flow in the life sciences, clean technology, software, and advanced manufacturing sectors.

Third, the restoration of SR&ED capital expenditures under paragraph 37(1)(b) and Section 127 for depreciable property acquired on or after December 16, 2024, requires hardware-intensive enterprises to institute rigorous asset-level tracking protocols. Claimants must document that newly acquired laboratory, prototyping, or computing equipment meets the 90%+ ("all or substantially all") SR&ED operating-time or value-consumption threshold (or between 50% and 90% for shared-use equipment), verify when the property becomes available for use under subsection 127(11.2), and evaluate the interaction between the 40%-refundable SR&ED capital ITC and Canada's Clean Economy ITCs—such as the 30% Clean Technology Manufacturing ITC, Clean Technology ITC, Clean Hydrogen ITC, and CCUS ITC—to maximize net present value while avoiding recapture exposure.

Finally, enterprises operating across multiple Canadian provinces should actively manage the government assistance interaction between provincial credits and the federal SR&ED pool. In Québec, companies with taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, should restructure their project tracking to capture both core R&D and newly eligible pre-commercialization activities and capital outlays under the 30% and 20% refundable CRIC regime, while carefully monitoring employee time allocation for the per-employee exclusion threshold. In Ontario and Manitoba, where non-refundable provincial tax credits (such as Ontario's 3.5% ORDTC on Schedule 508 or the non-refundable half of Manitoba's 15% credit) reduce the federal 35% refundable expenditure pool as government assistance in the year earned, pre-profitable CCPCs and ECPCs should evaluate executing timely statutory waivers or renunciations of non-refundable provincial credits to maximize immediate federal cash refunds.
